value.overview: The Western Gull (Larus occidentalis) is a large Pacific coast gull of western North America. It is strongly associated with rocky shorelines, beaches, bays, fishing areas, and offshore waters. Adults have a white head and underparts, a dark gray back, black wingtips, pink legs, and a large yellow bill marked with red. The species is resident or dispersive across most of its normal range and is only an exceptional visitor to Costa Rica.
value.classification: The Western Gull belongs to the gull family Laridae and the order Charadriiformes. It is closely related to other large North American gulls, including the Glaucous-winged Gull and California Gull.
value.identification: Adults are large, heavy-bodied gulls with a white head, neck, breast, and underparts; dark gray upperparts; black wingtips with small white markings; pink legs; and a thick yellow bill with a red spot near the tip. The eye is usually dark. Immature birds are mottled brown and gradually acquire adult plumage over several years. Western Gulls can resemble American Herring Gulls, but are generally bulkier and have darker mantles and heavier bills.
value.rangeHabitat: Western Gulls breed mainly along the Pacific coast from British Columbia through the western United States to Baja California, Mexico, using offshore rocks, islands, cliffs, beaches, and protected coastal sites. They forage in coastal waters, estuaries, bays, tidal zones, beaches, and around fishing operations. In Costa Rica, the species is recorded only as an accidental or highly unusual visitor, principally in coastal settings; it is not a regular resident or expected component of the country's gull fauna.
value.migrationStatus: Generally resident, with local and seasonal dispersal away from breeding colonies. In Costa Rica it is an accidental vagrant rather than a regular migrant, and records are exceptional.
value.breeding: Breeding usually occurs from spring into summer in dense colonies or loose groups on coastal islands, cliffs, headlands, and other protected shoreline sites. The nest is a shallow scrape lined with vegetation or debris. Usually two or three eggs are laid, and both adults defend the territory and feed the young. Incubation lasts about a month, and chicks generally fledge at roughly six weeks, although they remain dependent on adults for some time afterward.
value.dietFeeding: Western Gulls eat fish, squid, crabs, other marine invertebrates, seabird eggs and young, carrion, and discarded food. They forage by swimming, plunging or dipping at the surface, walking along beaches, scavenging around fishing vessels and ports, and taking prey from intertidal areas. Their flexible diet allows them to use both natural coastal habitats and human-modified shorelines.
value.behavior: This species is social outside the breeding season but strongly territorial around nests. It is powerful and maneuverable in flight, often soaring over beaches and headlands or resting on the sea. Western Gulls have loud, repeated calls and conspicuous courtship displays involving postures, calling, and food presentation. They commonly follow fishing boats, gather at refuse sites, and defend food or nesting space aggressively against other gulls and predators.

conservation.populationTrend: The species remains fairly common across much of its range, but available North American monitoring indicates a long-term decline, with especially concerning recent losses in parts of the population.
conservation.threats: Potential pressures include reduced availability of marine prey, changes in ocean conditions and El Niño-related food shortages, pollution, disturbance at breeding colonies, entanglement or bycatch, and contamination from marine debris. Historical pesticide effects, including DDT-related reproductive problems, also affected some populations.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect coastal nesting islands, cliffs, and foraging areas from disturbance, especially during the breeding season. Support clean fisheries and measures that reduce seabird bycatch, keep plastic and fishing line out of the ocean, avoid feeding gulls, and report unusual records in Costa Rica with clear photographs and location details to a recognized bird-recording platform or local ornithological organization.
